name: Syria
card_headline: Damascus has taken over the Kurdish-led northeast and shed most US sanctions, but Israel holds ground in the south, Suwayda is deadlocked and fuel hikes spark protests.
card_summary: President Ahmed al-Sharaa's government took the Kurdish-led northeast from the SDF in January, and the last US-held bases passed to Damascus in April.[1][2] The US repealed the Caesar Act in December 2025.[3] Israel still holds a buffer zone in the south, and Druze armed groups control security in Suwayda city.[4][5] The UN counts 15.6 million people needing aid, and fuel price hikes in September set off protests.[6][7]
card_local: Enab Baladi reports that SNHR counted at least 428 civilian deaths in the first half of 2026 and that clashes near Suwayda in July killed two National Guard members.[8][9] Local sourcing is thin in this draft: all four local sources are one outlet.
card_international: AP reports the first sitting of the People's Assembly on 12 July and Saudi investment deals, and Reuters reports the UN finding that at least 1,707 people were killed in Suwayda in 2025.[10][11][12]
card_scholar: Carnegie's Sima Beitinjaneh argues that patronage around the president echoes Assad-era patterns, and the Wilson Center's Jill Jermano says sanctions relief alone will not draw investment while money-laundering and corruption problems remain.[13][14]
context_md: A coalition overthrew Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, and Ahmed al-Sharaa leads the interim government.[1] A temporary constitution from March 2025 gives the People's Assembly lawmaking power for a renewable 30-month term.[15] The UN commission of inquiry reported more than 1,400 people killed on the coast in March 2025, mostly Alawite civilians, and the UN counted at least 1,707 killed in Suwayda in July 2025.[16][12] Real GDP fell nearly 53 percent between 2010 and 2022, and the World Bank puts reconstruction costs at $216 billion.[17] The US repealed the Caesar Act sanctions in December 2025.[3] In January 2026 government forces seized large areas from the SDF, which agreed on 30 January to integrate into the army.[1] Israel seized the UN-mandated buffer zone in southern Syria in December 2024 and has stayed.[4]

sections.title: The People's Assembly: two thirds chosen by electors, one third by the president
sections.body_md:
Syria's first parliamentary vote since Assad's fall, held on 5 October 2025, was indirect. About 7,000 members of electoral colleges across 60 districts chose 140 of the 210 seats, and interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa appoints the other 70.[18] Voting was postponed indefinitely in Suwayda and in Hasakah and Raqqa, which were then outside Damascus's control.[18] More than a dozen NGOs said in a joint statement that Sharaa could shape a loyal majority. Bassam Alahmad of Syrians for Truth and Justice said the process should not be called elections. Sharaa argues that direct elections are not feasible because many Syrians lack documents after displacement.[18]

Sharaa named his 70 appointees on 1 July 2026, including 15 women, which raised the number of women in the chamber to 21 from six. Seats for Suwayda were postponed.[15] The assembly held its first session on 12 July and elected Abdul Hamid al-Awak, a former Justice Ministry judge from Hasakah, as speaker with 99 votes.[10][19] Under the 2025 constitutional declaration it holds legislative authority for a renewable 30 months until a permanent constitution is adopted, and the government does not need a confidence vote. Rights groups warned that the framework concentrates influence over parliament in the presidency.[15]

Sima Beitinjaneh of Carnegie argues that the transitional government shows patronage patterns like those of the Assad era. She says the president's brothers hold senior economic and presidential posts, contracts are awarded without public tenders, and the Sovereign Wealth Fund has published no investment strategy. Carnegie does not take institutional positions, and several of her claims about business control are framed as reported rather than confirmed.[13]

lenses.international: AP and Al Jazeera report the indirect vote, the 70 presidential appointees and the 12 July first session.[10][18]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie's Beitinjaneh and Haid Haid, quoted by Al Jazeera as a Chatham House and Arab Reform Initiative analyst, both point to weak oversight and patronage in how seats and posts are filled.[13][18]

sections.title: The SDF lost its enclave in weeks, and Damascus now holds the northeast and its ISIS prisons
sections.body_md:
Damascus launched an offensive against the SDF in January 2026 and in about three weeks took large areas of northern and northeastern Syria that the SDF had held.[1] Clashes in Aleppo killed at least 23 people and displaced tens of thousands before the SDF pulled out of Deir Hafer.[20] The EUAA, analysing ACLED data, puts deaths in the January government-SDF fighting at roughly 250 to more than 300, mostly combatants.[21] A ceasefire announced on 18 January required the SDF to withdraw west of the Euphrates, integrate into the army and hand over border crossings and oil and gas fields.[22] On 30 January the sides announced a phased integration: three SDF brigades in one division, a fourth in Kobani tied to Aleppo governorate, and Kurdish-led institutions merged into the state. A March 2025 deal had made little progress.[1]

The prison and camp system moved with the territory. On 21 January the US military said it had moved 150 detainees from a Hasakah facility to Iraq, and that up to 7,000 people with alleged ISIL links could eventually be moved. Al-Hol, with about 24,000 residents, came under government control after the SDF withdrew.[23] The final US convoy left Qasrak air base on 16 April, and US Central Command said it had turned over all major bases in a conditions-based transition. Damascus says the handover reflects the SDF's absorption into national structures.[2] Syria's defense minister met the commander of the anti-ISIS coalition on 12 November.[24]

On 16 January Sharaa issued a decree recognising Kurdish as a national language, restoring citizenship to Kurds stripped of it in the 1962 Hasakah census and making Nowruz a paid holiday. The Kurdish-led administration called it a first step and said rights need permanent constitutions, not temporary decrees.[20] On 16 November students at Rojava University in Qamishlo protested a planned merger with the state-run Al Furat University, fearing less Kurdish-language teaching.[24]

lenses.international: Al Jazeera and Reuters carry the ceasefire, the integration deal and the US base handover.[22][1][2]
lenses.scholar: Charles Lister of the Middle East Institute framed three paths in a February podcast: consolidation, hybrid control or renewed conflict.[25] The EUAA says the January clashes did not become a prolonged conflict.[21]

sections.title: Two 2025 massacres, government inquiries and a Suwayda standoff that is not resolved
sections.body_md:
The UN Commission of Inquiry reported more than 1,400 people killed in March 2025 in Latakia, Tartus, Homs and Hama, mostly Alawite civilians.[16] Human Rights Watch, working with Syrians for Truth and Justice and Syrian Archive, found that the Defense Ministry centrally coordinated the operation. It found no direct evidence that senior officials ordered abuses, but said they failed to stop them.[26] A national Fact-Finding Committee counted 1,426 killed and referred 298 suspects to prosecutors, according to HRW, which says no senior official had been charged when it published.[26] The UN commission said 14 suspects had been arrested and prosecuted and that vetting and security-sector reform remain insufficient.[16]

For Suwayda, the commission counted at least 1,707 killed, mostly Druze civilians, along with Bedouin and at least 225 government personnel. It said government forces, tribal fighters and Druze armed groups all committed violations, some possibly war crimes, and attributed to the state the actions of tribal fighters who accompanied government forces early on. A government-appointed committee reported 1,760 deaths and 2,188 injuries from all sides and said many government personnel involved had been arrested. Up to 155,000 people remain displaced.[12] Damascus welcomed the commission's report and pledged public trials open to independent observers.[16]

Little has moved in Suwayda itself. The Druze Higher Legal Committee says at least 230 people are missing, and factions linked to Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, operating as the National Guard, control security decisions in Suwayda city and reject a US-sponsored roadmap agreed in Amman in September 2025.[5] The New Arab relays a December Washington Post report, citing officials, that Israel has backed Hijri's forces.[5] Israel says it wants to protect Syria's Druze.[27] On 2 and 3 July 2026 fighting near Tal Hadid killed two National Guard members. State-run al-Ikhbariya said the Guard attacked Internal Security Forces positions, and the Guard said it repelled a government attack.[9]

lenses.local: Enab Baladi relays the government's statement welcoming the UN report and reports the July Suwayda clashes with the competing accounts.[16][9]
lenses.international: Reuters reports the UN commission's Suwayda toll and the government committee's figure of 1,760 deaths.[12]
lenses.scholar: HRW's September 2025 report finds central coordination of the coastal operation by the Defense Ministry and no charges against senior officials at the time it published.[26]

sections.title: Violence is lower than in 2025, but ISIS cells, Assad loyalists and landmines still kill
sections.body_md:
SNHR documented at least 428 civilian deaths in the first half of 2026, falling from 111 in January to 41 in June. It attributes 202 to unidentified gunfire, 59 to landmines of unknown origin, 57 to the SDF, 12 to government forces, 9 to remnants of the Assad regime and 3 to ISIS. Eighty of the dead were children.[8] UN Deputy Special Envoy Claudio Cordone said March 2026 had the lowest level of direct conflict-related violence in 15 years, according to the EUAA.[21]

The EUAA reports that ISIS activity fell after December 2024, rose after a February 2026 call to confront the government, and declined from late March or early April. Authorities say they have arrested hundreds of suspects and dismantled dozens of cells.[21] On 23 February ISIS claimed attacks that killed at least five security personnel in Deir ez-Zor. On 24 February clashes near Jableh in Latakia killed at least four people in a fight between security forces and a group called Saraya al-Jawad, which the Interior Ministry accuses of assassinations and bombings.[28] Syrian security forces dismantled an ISIS cell in Aleppo on 12 November and arrested four members.[24]

Sectarian tension persists on the coast and in Homs. A bombing at a Homs mosque on 26 December 2025 killed at least eight people, and Saraya Ansar al-Sunna claimed it on Telegram. Alawite protests followed on 28 December, with the religious figure Ghazal Ghazal calling for political federalism from abroad. SANA reported four people killed in Latakia, and the Interior Ministry reported one officer killed.[29]

lenses.local: Enab Baladi reports the SNHR tally, including 59 deaths from landmines of unknown origin.[8]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera reports the February attacks in Latakia and Deir ez-Zor and the December protests.[28][29]
lenses.scholar: The EUAA describes the situation as fragile with signs of stabilisation.[21]

sections.title: Israel holds a buffer zone in the south, talks keep stalling, and Russia is scaling back its bases
sections.body_md:
Israel seized the UN-mandated buffer zone in December 2024, about 235 square kilometres, and later declared the 1974 disengagement agreement void, according to AP. It says its presence guards its northern border against Hezbollah. Sharaa has demanded that Israel withdraw.[4] SNHR counted at least 453 Israeli ground incursions between December 2024 and 6 October 2026, with at least 69 deaths and 162 arbitrary detentions. SANA, the state news agency, reported 125 incursions and 55 temporary checkpoints in Quneitra in October alone, and said Israeli vehicles entered Jabata al-Khashab on 13 November and detained three people. Israel's stated position is that its expanded presence is needed for its security.[30] AP reports that 49 Syrians have been detained since December 2024 and 16 released, according to Syrian officials and UN-backed investigators. The Israeli military says it detains only on reasonable suspicion of terrorism and denies abuse.[4]

US-mediated talks in Paris in early January produced a joint communication cell for intelligence sharing and de-escalation but no withdrawal timeline.[27] The talks froze in late February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, and resumed in Jordan on 24 August, where Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani met an Israeli delegation. No agreement was reported. Syria wants Israel back at its pre-8 December 2024 positions. Israel's reported red lines include blocking Turkish military activity in Syria.[31]

On 9 August Damascus announced a deal with Russia under which Russian facilities become joint training centres within three months, Syria takes over Latakia airport and Russia keeps access to Tartus. The National reports that about 1,000 Russian soldiers remained after most troops and hardware left. A Syrian official, unnamed in the report, called the deal part of an "American clean-up".[32]

lenses.local: SANA, a state outlet, carries Quneitra's monthly incursion tally. Independent Syrian reporting on the south was not read for this draft.[30]
lenses.international: AP and Al Jazeera report the detentions, the Paris communication cell and the stalled Jordan talks.[4][27][31]
lenses.scholar: Analyst Hassan Mneimneh doubted the August talks would ease tensions, and Waiel Olwan of the Jusoor institute said the Russia deal restores sovereign rights while preserving minimal Russian interests.[31][32]

sections.title: Sanctions are largely gone, but fuel prices, a weak banking system and patronage drive the economic story
sections.body_md:
The US repealed the Caesar Act in December 2025 without conditions, though Congress will receive periodic reports on minority rights and counterterrorism.[3] President Trump announced in July 2026 that Syria would come off the state sponsor of terrorism list.[33] The Wilson Center's Jill Jermano writes that the designation was rescinded in August, that the UN Security Council removed HTS sanctions in February, that the central bank has reconnected to SWIFT, and that Visa and Mastercard began processing in Syria in September. She adds that Syria remains on the FATF grey list and that the Commercial Bank of Syria still carries a 2004 US money-laundering designation.[14] The National reported on 11 August that Congress had not yet decided on the designation move.[32]

The World Bank puts reconstruction at $216 billion, within a range of $140 billion to $345 billion, nearly ten times projected 2024 GDP of $21.4 billion. Real GDP fell nearly 53 percent between 2010 and 2022.[17] After a July visit, IMF staff expect double-digit growth in 2026. They say inflation has picked up considerably this year, a dysfunctional banking system constrains monetary policy and poverty remains widespread. The findings are preliminary and will not go to the IMF Board.[34]

Foreign money is arriving. AP reports Saudi deals in February including a telecom cable project of nearly $1 billion led by STC and a new airport for Aleppo.[11] Chevron and Qatar's UCC Holdings agreed in May to explore for offshore oil and gas, and on 17 July Syrian and Iraqi state oil companies signed memoranda to revive the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline after Iraq's exports collapsed following the strikes on Iran that began on 28 February.[35]

At home, a decree raised diesel by 40 percent and petrol by 28 percent on 13 and 14 September. Since February, 95-octane petrol is up about 86 percent and diesel has more than doubled. Protests spread from Aleppo and Idlib to Hama and Daraa. The government calls the rises temporary and blames international fuel prices, and the Energy Ministry says Syria produces about 100,000 barrels a day against demand of 300,000 to 325,000. About 130 new pounds buy a dollar.[7]

lenses.international: AP reports the Caesar Act repeal and the Saudi deals, and Al Jazeera reports on the fuel protests from Damascus.[3][11][7]
lenses.scholar: The Wilson Center says sanctions relief is necessary but not sufficient, and Carnegie says the Sovereign Wealth Fund and the procurement committee operate with little published information.[14][13]

sections.title: 15.6 million people need aid as drought and funding cuts meet more than 3.5 million returns
sections.body_md:
The 2026 humanitarian plan counts 15.6 million people in need, 6.6 percent fewer than in 2025. It reports 13.3 million food-insecure Syrians, about 7.2 million of them acutely, and says at least 25 percent live in extreme poverty and 67 percent below $3.65 a day. The 2025 drought was the most severe in nearly 40 years, damaged 95 percent of rainfed crops and left a wheat deficit of 2.7 million tons.[6]

UNHCR counted 5,542,227 internally displaced people in April 2026. Since December 2024, 1,630,874 refugees and 1,890,390 displaced people have returned. Its 2026 operation was 35 percent funded.[36] By the end of May the return figures were about 1.67 million and 1.92 million. Jordan's weekly returns fell to 1,000 to 1,300 from about 3,000 in 2025, and about 2.26 million Syrians remain in Turkiye under temporary protection. Barriers include damaged housing, weak services, explosive ordnance and missing documents.[37]

WFP says it has halved emergency food assistance for lack of funds, cut operations from 14 governorates to seven and ended a bread subsidy that reached up to 4 million people daily in some areas. It needs $189 million over six months. Country director Marianne Ward said the cuts are driven solely by funding, not by lower needs.[38] UN officials told the Security Council on 16 November that Syria shows signs of progress that explosive ordnance, winter and funding gaps threaten.[39]

lenses.international: UN briefings relayed on 16 November describe progress threatened by funding shortfalls, and WFP reports the cuts.[39][38]
lenses.scholar: UNHCR's regional survey work finds return intentions have risen but many refugees are waiting to see, notably in Turkiye.[37]

sections.title: Press freedom rose 36 places, journalists were detained in Aleppo, and 181,677 people remain detained or missing
sections.body_md:
RSF ranks Syria 141st of 180 in its 2026 index, up from 177th in 2025, the largest rise in the table. RSF calls the gains fragile, and safety and security is the weakest indicator at 154th.[40][41] In January, CPJ reported that government forces detained three journalists in Aleppo's Sheikh Maqsoud and Ashrafiyah neighborhoods on 10 January: Rudaw's Vivyan Fetah and Aland Issa for about 90 minutes, and Syria TV's Adnan Emam for about 12 hours. An anonymous freelancer told CPJ that independent outlets were blocked while government-aligned outlets, including Al Jazeera and TRT, were allowed in. The Information Ministry's Omar Haj Ahmed said restrictions were for safety, called Emam's detention routine and said reports on Fetah were incorrect. The ministry called CPJ's report "replete with inaccuracies", and CPJ said it stands by its reporting.[42]

HRW said in February that the government created bodies on transitional justice and missing persons but gave little transparency about senior officials' roles in the 2025 violence, and that Syria still needs a legal framework for international crimes and command responsibility.[43] SNHR documents at least 181,677 people detained, forcibly disappeared or of unknown fate between March 2011 and June 2026, and 45,364 deaths from torture or harsh detention, about 99 percent of them in former regime facilities.[8]

lenses.local: Enab Baladi reports the RSF rise, with Syria ranked tenth of 22 Arab countries according to rights defender Mansour al-Omari.[40]
lenses.international: CPJ's account of the Aleppo detentions is disputed by the Information Ministry.[42]
lenses.scholar: HRW urges authorities to examine abuses by all sides before and after December 2024, saying the effort cannot be selective or one-sided.[43]

timeline.text: Assad is overthrown; Israel seizes the UN-mandated buffer zone in the south.
Government forces and aligned groups begin killings in Alawite-majority areas of the coast; the UN reports more than 1,400 dead.
Violence begins in Suwayda; the UN later counts at least 1,707 dead.
Indirect parliamentary vote: electoral colleges choose 140 of 210 seats.
World Bank puts reconstruction costs at $216 billion.
The US repeals the Caesar Act sanctions.
Sharaa issues a decree recognising Kurdish language and citizenship rights.
Government and SDF announce a ceasefire after about three weeks of fighting.
SDF and Damascus announce a phased integration agreement.
The last US convoy leaves Qasrak air base; Syria takes control of all former US bases.
The People's Assembly holds its first session.
Damascus announces a deal with Russia to scale back its military facilities.
Syria and Israel hold US-mediated talks in Jordan; no agreement reported.
A decree raises diesel prices 40 percent and petrol 28 percent; protests spread.
AP reports 49 Syrians detained by Israel since December 2024.
Syria hosts a partnership forum in Damascus; the EU says it expects to sign a $192 million support package.

factchecks.claim: Syria remains under sweeping US sanctions that block reconstruction.
factchecks.by: Common framing in coverage of Syria's economy
factchecks.evidence: The US repealed the Caesar Act in December 2025, and the Wilson Center says Syria's state sponsor of terrorism designation and HTS's terrorist designation were rescinded in August 2026. Investment barriers remain: the Wilson Center lists the FATF grey list, a 2004 US money-laundering designation on the Commercial Bank of Syria and corruption concerns, and Al Jazeera reports that earlier relief has not transformed the economy.

factchecks.by: Official description of the 5 October 2025 vote as parliamentary elections
factchecks.evidence: About 7,000 electoral college members chose 140 of 210 seats, the president appoints the other 70, and voting was postponed in Suwayda, Hasakah and Raqqa. Sharaa says direct elections are not feasible because many Syrians lack documents. A joint NGO statement and Syrians for Truth and Justice dispute the label. The assembly's 30-month term is renewable and no popular election date was found in this draft.

scores.coverage_basis: AP files from Damascus, and Reuters, AFP and Al Jazeera report regularly, with spikes around the January offensive, the sanctions repeal and the Israel talks.[11][12][1] Think-tank and UN output is steady, from Carnegie and the Wilson Center to UNHCR and the EUAA.[13][14][36][21] Syrian outlets such as Enab Baladi publish regularly, but this draft reads few of them.[8]

severity.basis: SNHR counted at least 428 civilian deaths in the first half of 2026, and the EUAA reports the UN's Cordone saying March 2026 was the lowest month of direct conflict violence in 15 years, while Suwayda is in military stalemate.[8][21]
15.6 million people need aid, 5.5 million are displaced and WFP has halved emergency food aid for lack of funding.[6][36][38]

Parliament is two thirds indirectly chosen and one third appointed, HRW finds little transparency on senior officials' roles in the 2025 killings, and RSF ranks press freedom 141st of 180, up 36 places.[18][43][40]
Reconstruction costs are nearly ten times 2024 GDP, the IMF notes inflation picked up in 2026 and the banking system is dysfunctional, and September fuel hikes set off protests.[17][34][7]
Sanctions relief, falling violence after January and refugee returns point up, while fuel protests, the Suwayda standoff and stalled Israel talks point down.[3][21][37][7][31]

parts.basis: The US handed its bases to Damascus in April, Russia is scaling back its bases, Saudi Arabia is signing investment deals, and Israel struck an Idlib airbase it said Turkish troops would use, which Syria and Turkey deny.[2][32][11][31]
Syria is positioned as an alternative route for Iraqi oil after the strikes on Iran, but its own economy is small, with 2024 nominal GDP of $21.4 billion.[35][17]
Israeli incursions run through Quneitra and Daraa, ISIS detainees and camps are a cross-border risk, and returns shape Lebanon, Jordan and Turkiye.[30][23][37]
About 1.67 million refugees have returned, while about 2.26 million Syrians remain in Turkiye under temporary protection.[37]

The UN Security Council removed HTS sanctions in February 2026, the US moved to lift the state sponsor designation, and the UN commission found possible war crimes by several parties in Suwayda.[14][12]

summary: Syria matters beyond its borders through the Israel front, Gulf and Turkish investment, the future of ISIS detention and the return of refugees, more than through trade.[30][11][23][37]
gi.up: A collapse of the Israel talks into wider fighting, an ISIS breakout from detention facilities, or renewed war in Suwayda or the northeast.
gi.down: A signed Israel-Syria security agreement, steady refugee returns and no new mass-casualty violence.

gaps: Local sourcing is thin: all four local sources are Enab Baladi, which carried no bylines. SANA, Syria TV, Syria Direct, North Press, Suwayda local outlets and Kurdish outlets were not read directly; Al-Ikhbariya and SANA claims arrive through other outlets.

Heavy reliance on Al Jazeera (Qatar state-funded, flagged) for events; AP and Reuters are used where they were found. The Iraqi News report on 16 November army deployments in former Kurdish-held areas could not be opened.

The Crisis Group November 2025 report on the coast and Suwayda was not readable (only a course-site link to the PDF), and ACLED was read only through the EUAA summary. The UN commission reports (A/HRC/61) were not opened; their figures come from Reuters, Enab Baladi and the EUAA.

Suwayda death counts differ: at least 1,707 (UN via Reuters), 1,760 (government-appointed committee), at least 1,700 (EUAA) and 'more than 1,500' in Enab Baladi's summary of the Foreign Ministry statement. Coast deaths: more than 1,400 (UN, HRW) and 1,426 (government Fact-Finding Committee, via HRW).

January 2026 fighting deaths (roughly 250 to more than 300) come from the EUAA's analysis of ACLED and MEI, not from a direct count. The current state of SDF integration after April was not established.

The state sponsor of terrorism removal is described three ways: announced by Trump in July (Al Jazeera), not yet decided by Congress on 11 August (The National), and rescinded in August (Wilson Center). The exact date and mechanism were not confirmed.

No source was read on electricity supply, Captagon, chemical weapons, Turkey's role in the north, Lebanon border security, or how the Iran war affects Syria beyond the pipeline plans and the freeze in Israel talks.
Poverty figures differ in basis: HRW over 90 percent, a UN estimate of nearly 90 percent (via Al Jazeera), and 67 percent below $3.65 a day in the OCHA plan. They were not reconciled.

The Israeli detainee count (49) is AP citing Syrian officials and UN-backed investigators, and the Quneitra incursion figures come from SANA through one article. The Washington Post report on Israeli backing of Hijri's forces is relayed by The New Arab and was not read directly.

Several pages show no date: the Al Arabiya parliament piece, the WFP cuts statement, the OCHA plan and the UNHCR update. Dates come from URLs. The title of The National's Russia report was not retrieved.
No date for a popular election or for the permanent constitution was found. SNHR data after June 2026 and Syria's second-half 2026 casualty figures were not located.

No named Syria-based local reporter could be verified from an opened page; the reporters listed are bylines on pages that were opened, and several write from outside Syria. The Lawfare episode length was not shown.
Podcast and documentary links point to listing pages; availability varies by country. The FRONTLINE documentary aired in July 2025 and predates the 2026 events.

local_md:
Enab Baladi relays the government's statement welcoming the UN report and reports the July Suwayda clashes with the competing accounts.[16][9]

Enab Baladi reports the SNHR tally, including 59 deaths from landmines of unknown origin.[8]

SANA, a state outlet, carries Quneitra's monthly incursion tally. Independent Syrian reporting on the south was not read for this draft.[30]

Enab Baladi reports the RSF rise, with Syria ranked tenth of 22 Arab countries according to rights defender Mansour al-Omari.[40]
international_md:
AP and Al Jazeera report the indirect vote, the 70 presidential appointees and the 12 July first session.[10][18]

Al Jazeera and Reuters carry the ceasefire, the integration deal and the US base handover.[22][1][2]

Reuters reports the UN commission's Suwayda toll and the government committee's figure of 1,760 deaths.[12]

Al Jazeera reports the February attacks in Latakia and Deir ez-Zor and the December protests.[28][29]

AP and Al Jazeera report the detentions, the Paris communication cell and the stalled Jordan talks.[4][27][31]

AP reports the Caesar Act repeal and the Saudi deals, and Al Jazeera reports on the fuel protests from Damascus.[3][11][7]

UN briefings relayed on 16 November describe progress threatened by funding shortfalls, and WFP reports the cuts.[39][38]

CPJ's account of the Aleppo detentions is disputed by the Information Ministry.[42]
scholar_md:
Carnegie's Beitinjaneh and Haid Haid, quoted by Al Jazeera as a Chatham House and Arab Reform Initiative analyst, both point to weak oversight and patronage in how seats and posts are filled.[13][18]

Charles Lister of the Middle East Institute framed three paths in a February podcast: consolidation, hybrid control or renewed conflict.[25] The EUAA says the January clashes did not become a prolonged conflict.[21]

HRW's September 2025 report finds central coordination of the coastal operation by the Defense Ministry and no charges against senior officials at the time it published.[26]

The EUAA describes the situation as fragile with signs of stabilisation.[21]

Analyst Hassan Mneimneh doubted the August talks would ease tensions, and Waiel Olwan of the Jusoor institute said the Russia deal restores sovereign rights while preserving minimal Russian interests.[31][32]

The Wilson Center says sanctions relief is necessary but not sufficient, and Carnegie says the Sovereign Wealth Fund and the procurement committee operate with little published information.[14][13]

UNHCR's regional survey work finds return intentions have risen but many refugees are waiting to see, notably in Turkiye.[37]

HRW urges authorities to examine abuses by all sides before and after December 2024, saying the effort cannot be selective or one-sided.[43]
